models.family: feedforward neural network trained by Levenberg-Marquardt
models.purpose: Forecast the next-day and the longer-horizon price of gold and of bitcoin from seven days of prices.
models.summary: A standard backpropagation network whose gradient step is replaced by the Levenberg-Marquardt update, because the authors say plain gradient descent converges too slowly and falls into local optima. The MATLAB trainlm routine does the fitting. Gold uses ten hidden nodes and bitcoin sixteen, the data are split 70:15:15, and training stops at 1000 iterations or when the mean square error drops below a set value.

governing_equations.normalized_latex: H_j = f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} W_{ij} + a_j\right), \quad j = 1, 2, \ldots, L
governing_equations.purpose: Hidden-node output. The input is not multiplied by the weight; the sum is printed over the weights alone.

governing_equations.normalized_latex: O_k = \sum_{j=1}^{n} W_{jk} H_j + b_k, \quad k = 1, 2, \ldots, m
governing_equations.purpose: Output-node value. The sum runs to n, the input count, rather than to L.
Prediction error used to drive the weight and threshold updates.

governing_equations.source_expression: W_{ij} = W_{ij} + eta H_j ((1 - H_j) x_i sum_{k=1}^{m} W_{jk} e_k ), i = 1..n; j = 1..L

governing_equations.purpose: Input-to-hidden weight update. The only equation in which the input x_i appears.

governing_equations.source_expression: W_{jk} = W_{jk} + eta H_j e_k, j = 1..L; k = 1..m
governing_equations.normalized_latex: W_{jk} = W_{jk} + \eta H_j e_k, \quad j=1,\ldots,L;\; k=1,\ldots,m

equation_status.reason: Equations (1) through (6) are printed in section 4.1.1 and were read off the rendered pages.

objectives: Minimize the mean square error between the predicted price and the actual price.
constraints: The model may use only prices known on or before the trading day.
Training stops when the mean square error falls below a set value or the iteration count reaches 1000.

details: Weights and thresholds are drawn at random from the interval (-1, 1).

parameter_estimation.method: Levenberg-Marquardt through the MATLAB trainlm routine, which the authors decline to derive.

steps: Choose the number of layers and hidden nodes by trial.
Draw each weight and threshold from (-1, 1).
Compute the hidden outputs and the output-layer values.
Update both sets of weights and both thresholds.
Stop when the mean square error is below the set value.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Stop when the minimum mean square error drops below a set value, or after 1000 iterations. The set value is never printed.

assumptions: Price series are dynamic, nonlinear, and time-varying, which the authors take as the reason a neural network fits.
The activation function is left unnamed.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The fit is reported rather than derived: the coefficient of determination exceeds 0.99 on the training, test, validation, and full sets for gold, and the same is claimed for bitcoin.

models.computational_cost: One trainlm run per asset and per horizon, capped at 1000 iterations. No runtime is reported.
strengths: The authors say the Levenberg-Marquardt step converges faster than plain gradient descent.
Separate short and long horizons are kept for each asset.
limitations: Equation (1) sums the weights without multiplying by the input, so the hidden output does not depend on the data.
The activation function, the error threshold, and the damping term are never given values.
missing_details: The activation function f is unnamed.
The mean square error threshold that stops training is unnamed.
Algorithm 1 leaves several symbols undefined and is not transcribed as a governing equation.

models.family: threshold trading rule sized by the Sharpe ratio
models.purpose: Turn the price forecasts into a daily buy, hold, or sell decision and a portfolio value.
models.summary: The authors reject both the statistical and the black-box portfolio models because the only input is price, and they build a four-stage rule instead. The model waits until both assets have seven days of prices, buys when the forecast rise clears a threshold, sizes the purchase by the Sharpe ratio, and sells when the forecast turns down. Recomputing the forecast every day is what earns the model its name.

governing_equations.source_expression: Sharpe ratio = expected rate of return / std of gold or bitcoin over the past seven days
governing_equations.purpose: Risk measure used to split the cash between the two assets.
Portfolio after buying both assets on the same day. The factors 0.99 and 0.98 are the only statement of the commission rates.
Portfolio after buying only gold, for a Sharpe ratio above one and below one.
Portfolio after buying only bitcoin, for a Sharpe ratio above one and below one.

equation_status.reason: Equation (7) and the three portfolio-state expressions are printed in section 4.2.2 and were read off the rendered page.

constraints: No purchase is made until both assets have seven days of prices.
No purchase is made when no cash is held.
Short selling is excluded by assumption 4.
Gold is bought when the next-day rise exceeds 2 percent or the five-day rise exceeds 3 percent.
Bitcoin is bought when the next-day rise exceeds 3.5 percent or the longer-horizon rise exceeds 4.5 percent.

details: The portfolio starts at one thousand dollars in cash and nothing in either asset, on 11 September 2016.

parameter_estimation.method: Grid search over the four thresholds, keeping the combination with the largest terminal profit.

steps: Accumulate seven days of prices for both assets before the first decision.
Buy when the forecast rise clears the asset's short or long threshold.
Compute the Sharpe ratio from the larger of the short return and half the long return.
If both assets qualify, split all the cash by the normalized Sharpe ratios.
If only one qualifies, spend all the cash when its Sharpe ratio exceeds one and its share otherwise.
Sell when both the next-day and the long forecast point down.
Update the asset value after every buy, sale, and hold.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: The rule runs once per trading day from 11 September 2016 to 10 September 2021. There is no iterative convergence.

assumptions: The traded amount is too small to move the market.
Decisions use only prices known that day.
The long-horizon holding is treated as riskier, so its return is halved inside the Sharpe ratio.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The threshold search returns 2, 3, 3.5, and 4.5 percent, the same values the model already used, and the rule finishes the period at 270836 dollars against five control strategies.

models.computational_cost: One pass over the trading days plus a grid over four short threshold lists. No runtime is reported.
strengths: The rule uses both horizons rather than one.
The position size falls as the Sharpe ratio falls, so risk changes the allocation.
limitations: The authors call the rule a greedy algorithm whose result may be only locally optimal.
The simulated trading concentrates on bitcoin and barely trades gold.
Algorithm 2 prints the buy and sell lines reversed relative to the prose.
missing_details: The selling-stage portfolio update is declared similar to the buying stage and not written out.
The page 16 grid labels the bitcoin long threshold beta_1, reusing the gold symbol.
The rewritten buying rule on page 19, the return exceeding one minus the square of one minus the commission ratio, is stated in prose and not given its own equation.

dependency_edges.handoff: The forecast prices O_k decide whether each asset's rise clears its threshold and supply the returns inside the Sharpe ratio.
